title: More About Spain, from Two Kisses to the Camino
summary: Spanish greetings, names, festivals, islands and the Camino all have clear reasons behind them, and you can use them in real conversations.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: In part one, we learned about the history, places and food of Spain. Today we will learn about kisses, names, a fire festival, islands and a long walk. Then we will practise three real conversations.

items.prompt: How do people say hello in your country?
Do you sit and talk at the table after a meal?
What is the longest walk you have ever done?

blocks.title: Part 1: Two Kisses to Say Hello
paragraphs: When people in Spain meet, they often give dos besos. Dos besos is Spanish for two kisses, one on each cheek. It is not a real kiss. The cheeks just touch. People make a small kiss sound in the air. Women do this with women, and men do it with women. People do it with friends and family. They also do it with someone new, like a friend of a friend.

Two men usually shake hands. If they are close friends or family, they often hug. At work, more people now shake hands, especially at a first meeting. For Spanish people, the two kisses are a normal, warm hello, like a smile. So a Spanish person may feel a little hurt if a visitor steps back.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: Two Kisses to Say Hello

items.prompt: How do two men usually say hello in Spain?
items.answer: They shake hands, or they hug if they are close.

rows.meaning: when you meet someone for the first time
rows.example: Hello, nice to meet you. I'm from Japan.

rows.meaning: when you tell people how you say hello in your country
rows.example: In Japan, we usually bow, but I like two kisses too.

blocks.title: Part 2: Two Family Names
paragraphs: Most people in Spain have one first name and two family names. The first family name usually comes from the father. The second family name comes from the mother. So one name shows both sides of the family. The famous painter Pablo Picasso shows this. His two family names were Ruiz and Picasso. Ruiz was his father's family name, and Picasso was his mother's. Later, he used only his mother's name.

When women in Spain marry, they do not change their names. They keep the family names from their parents all their lives. Today, parents can choose which family name comes first. But all the children in one family must have the same order. So brothers and sisters always have the same two family names.

items.prompt: Where did the two family names of Pablo Picasso come from?
items.answer: Ruiz came from his father, and Picasso came from his mother.

rows.meaning: when you want to hear all of someone's names
rows.example: What is your full name, with both family names?

rows.term: My first family name comes from my dad.
rows.meaning: when you say where your family names are from
rows.example: My second family name comes from my mum.

blocks.title: Part 3: Las Fallas, a Festival of Fire
paragraphs: Every March, the city of Valencia has a big festival called Las Fallas. Each part of the city makes a falla. A falla is a very big group of many figures. Each figure in a falla is a ninot. Fallas are made of wood and paper, and some are as tall as a building. Many are funny, because they make jokes about famous people and the news.

On the night of 19 March, people burn almost all of them. This fire night is called la Cremà. Why burn something so beautiful? The idea comes from carpenters, people who make things from wood. In winter, they used old wood to hold candles, so they could work at night. At the end of winter, the days got longer, so they burned the old wood. They did it on 19 March, the day of Saint Joseph. Saint Joseph also worked with wood, so he was special to them. Every year, visitors vote for their favourite ninot. The winners are saved from the fire and go to a museum.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: Las Fallas, a Festival of Fire

items.prompt: Why did people in Valencia first burn old wood in March?
items.answer: The days got longer, so they did not need it to work at night.

rows.term: What time does la Cremà start?
rows.meaning: when you ask when something starts
rows.example: What time does la Cremà start on 19 March?

rows.meaning: when you ask the reason for a custom
rows.example: It's so beautiful. Why do you burn it?

blocks.title: Part 4: The Canary Islands
paragraphs: The Canary Islands are seven big islands in the Atlantic Ocean. They are part of Spain, but only about 100 kilometres from Africa. The islands were made by volcanoes. The volcano Teide is on Tenerife, the biggest island. It is the highest mountain in Spain.

People call them the islands of eternal spring, a spring that never ends. The weather is warm all year, and it does not change much. Winters are warm, because the islands are far south. In summer, the sea is cool and the wind blows on most days. So winter and summer are not very different.

items.prompt: Why are the Canary Islands called the islands of eternal spring?
items.answer: The weather is warm all year, and winter and summer are not very different.

blocks.title: Part 5: The Camino de Santiago
paragraphs: Camino de Santiago is Spanish for the Way of Saint James. It is a long walk to the city of Santiago de Compostela. The city is in the north-west of Spain. Saint James was one of the first people to follow Jesus. People believe he is buried in the big church of the city. So for more than a thousand years, pilgrims have walked there. Pilgrims are people who travel to a special church or place. The most popular way starts in France and is about 800 kilometres long.

People on the Camino carry a pilgrim passport. In each town where they sleep, they get a stamp in it. The stamps show where they walked. At the end, pilgrims can get the Compostela. It is a special paper with their name on it. To get it, pilgrims must walk at least the last 100 kilometres. On this part, they need at least two stamps every day. That is why many people start in Sarria, just over 100 kilometres from Santiago.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: The Camino de Santiago

items.prompt: Why do many people start the walk in Sarria?
items.answer: It is just over 100 kilometres from Santiago, so pilgrims can get the Compostela.

rows.term: How much is a bed for one night?
rows.meaning: when you ask what a bed costs
rows.example: Hello! How much is a bed for one night?

rows.term: Can I have a stamp, please?
rows.meaning: when you want a stamp in your pilgrim passport
rows.example: Can I have a stamp, please? This is my first day.

rows.term: How far is it to Santiago?
rows.meaning: when you want to know how far a place is
rows.example: How far is it to Santiago from here?

blocks.title: Scene: Sunday Lunch with a Spanish Family
paragraphs: It is a Sunday in March, a few days before Las Fallas. Your friend Lucía invites you to lunch at her family's home in Valencia. In Spain, people often stay at the table after a meal and talk. This time is called the sobremesa. It is Spanish for over the table.
Your goal is to say hello and ask about names. Then make a plan for Las Fallas.

blocks.title: Conversation: Sunday Lunch with a Spanish Family

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Come in! This is my mum, Carmen, and this is my dad, Javier.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hello, nice to meet you.

turns.speaker: Carmen
turns.text: Nice to meet you too! Two kisses, the Spanish way.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: In Japan, we usually bow. But I like this!

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: Welcome to our home. Please sit down.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you. Lucía, what is your full name?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: It's Lucía Martínez García. Martínez comes from my dad, and García comes from my mum.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Carmen, did you change your family names when you married?

turns.speaker: Carmen
turns.text: No. Women in Spain keep their names. I am still Carmen García López.

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: Lunch is ready. It's Sunday, so we're having paella.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Do you eat paella every Sunday?

turns.speaker: Carmen
turns.text: Many Sundays, yes. Here in Valencia, paella is a family lunch. We never eat it at night.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Why not at night?

turns.speaker: Carmen
turns.text: Lunch is our big meal of the day. And paella takes a long time to cook. At night, we eat something small and light, so we sleep well.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: That was delicious. Should I go now?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: No, stay! Now it's the sobremesa. We sit and talk, often for hours.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What are your plans for Las Fallas?

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: On 19 March, we go to la Cremà. It's Saint Joseph's day, so it's also Father's Day in Spain.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Can I come with you?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Of course! Meet us at the City Hall Square at half past nine.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. See you on the 19th!

blocks.title: Scene: The Night of Fire in Valencia
paragraphs: It is the night of 19 March. The streets are full of people. A very big falla stands in the City Hall Square. You meet Lucía and Javier there.
Your goal is to ask when the fallas burn and why people burn them.

blocks.title: Conversation: The Night of Fire in Valencia

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hi, Lucía! Happy Father's Day, Javier!

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: Thank you!

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What time does la Cremà start?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: It starts with the children's fallas at eight. At ten, the big fallas all over the city burn.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: And this one?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: This is the City Hall falla. It burns last, at eleven.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Will they burn all the ninots?

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: Almost all. Visitors vote for their favourite ninot, and the winners go to the museum.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: But it's so beautiful. Why do you burn it?

turns.speaker: Javier
turns.text: It's like the carpenters long ago. At the end of winter, we burn the old things.

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: And when the fire ends, this year's Fallas end. Then next year's Fallas begin.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: So we wait here until eleven?

turns.speaker: Lucía
turns.text: Yes. Then we watch it burn!

blocks.title: Scene: Starting the Camino in Sarria
paragraphs: In summer, you arrive in Sarria to walk the last part of the Camino. You go to a pilgrim hostel, a cheap place where pilgrims sleep. Manuel works there.
Your goal is to get a bed and a pilgrim passport. Then ask about the walk.

blocks.title: Conversation: Starting the Camino in Sarria

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Hello! Do you have a bed for tonight?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: Yes, we do. Are you walking to Santiago?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Yes, I'm starting tomorrow. How much is a bed for one night?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: It's 10 euros. Pilgrims can stay here for one night only. Do you have a pilgrim passport?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Not yet. Where can I get one?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: You can buy one here. It's 2 euros.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Great. Can I have a stamp, please?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: Here you are, your first stamp. From here, you need two stamps every day.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: How far is it to Santiago?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: About 115 kilometres. People usually walk it in five days.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Where do people sleep tomorrow night?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: Many stop in Portomarín. It's 22 kilometres from here.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: And what do I do in Santiago?

turns.speaker: Manuel
turns.text: Go to the Pilgrim Office with your pilgrim passport. They give you the Compostela, and it's free.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: Thank you so much!

blocks.title: Speaking
paragraphs: Work with a partner. Choose one scene and act out the conversation. One of you is the visitor, and the other is Lucía, Carmen, Javier or Manuel. Then change roles. At the end, choose one Spanish custom and explain its reason to your partner.

blocks.title: Final Reflection
blocks.intro: Every hello, festival and place in this lesson has a reason.

items.prompt: Would you be happy to give two kisses to someone new?
Would you like two family names, one from each parent?
Would you like a long sobremesa after Sunday lunch?
Which would you choose: Las Fallas, Teide or the Camino?
What was the most interesting thing you learned today?
